hints: Think about what a voltmeter connected between two half-cells is actually measuring when no current flows.
Recall the three standard condition values that must be stated for concentrations, temperature and gas pressure.
walkthrough:
Picture what is being measured**
Imagine you join two different half-cells with a wire and a high resistance voltmeter. Electrons want to flow from the more negative half-cell to the more positive one. The voltage you read is the difference between the two electrode potentials. That difference is the cell potential.

Add the word standard**
Standard simply means you compare fairly. Every solution that takes part must be $1 \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$, the temperature must be $298 \text{ K}$ ($25^{\circ}\text{C}$) and any gas must be at $1 \text{ atm}$ pressure. Only then is the value $E^{\ominus}_{cell}$.

Final answer: The potential difference between two half-cells / electrodes.
Measured under standard conditions of $1 \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$ for all solutions, $298 \text{ K}$ and $1 \text{ atm}$ for gases.

hints: Check whether either half-cell contains a solid metal that can conduct electrons to the external circuit.
walkthrough:
Spot why a normal metal electrode will not work**
A $\text{Co}^{3+}/\text{Co}^{2+}$ half-cell is just a mixture of two ions in solution. A $\text{Cl}_{2}/\text{Cl}^{-}$ half-cell is a gas bubbled into a solution of its ions. Neither contains a solid metal to carry electrons in and out, so you must add an unreactive conductor.

Choose the inert conductor**
Platinum is inert, conducts well and does not take part in the redox change. So a Pt wire or foil is placed in the $\text{Co}^{3+}/\text{Co}^{2+}$ solution and another Pt electrode is used for the $\text{Cl}_{2}/\text{Cl}^{-}$ half-cell, with $\text{Cl}_{2}$ gas bubbled over its surface.
Final answer: Both electrodes are platinum (Pt).

hints: Look up $E^{\ominus}$ for $\text{Co}^{3+}/\text{Co}^{2+}$ (+1.82 V) and for $\text{Cl}_{2}/\text{Cl}^{-}$ (+1.36 V) and subtract the less positive from the more positive.
walkthrough:
Pick out the two $E^{\ominus}$ values**
From the Data Booklet, $E^{\ominus}(\text{Co}^{3+}/\text{Co}^{2+}) = +1.82 \text{ V}$ and $E^{\ominus}(\text{Cl}_{2}/\text{Cl}^{-}) = +1.36 \text{ V}$. The cobalt half-cell is more positive, so it will be reduced and the chlorine half-cell will be oxidised.

Subtract to get the cell potential**
Use $$E^{\ominus}_{cell} = E^{\ominus}_{positive} - E^{\ominus}_{negative}$$ $$E^{\ominus}_{cell} = 1.82 - 1.36 = +0.46 \text{ V}$$ The positive sign confirms the reaction is feasible under standard conditions.

hints: Decide which species is reduced ($\text{Co}^{3+}$ to $\text{Co}^{2+}$) and which is oxidised ($\text{Cl}^{-}$ to $\text{Cl}_{2}$), then balance electrons.
walkthrough:
Write the two half-equations in the correct direction**
Reduction at the positive electrode: $\text{Co}^{3+} + \text{e}^{-} \rightarrow \text{Co}^{2+}$. Oxidation at the negative electrode: $2\text{Cl}^{-} \rightarrow \text{Cl}_{2} + 2\text{e}^{-}$.

Cancel the electrons**
Multiply the cobalt equation by 2 to give $2\text{e}^{-}$, then add: $$2\text{Co}^{3+} + 2\text{Cl}^{-} \rightarrow \text{Cl}_{2} + 2\text{Co}^{2+}$$ Charges and atoms both balance, $+4$ on each side.

hints: Start with $Q = It$ to find the total charge, remembering to convert 30 minutes to seconds, then use $F = 96500 \text{ C mol}^{-1}$ to find moles of electrons.
Use the given half-equation to link 6 moles of electrons to 1 mole of $\text{CO}_{2}$, then multiply moles of $\text{CO}_{2}$ by $24000 \text{ cm}^{3} \text{ mol}^{-1}$ for room conditions.
walkthrough:
Convert current and time into charge**
Charge is current times time in seconds. Think of it as the total electrons pushed round the circuit: $$Q = It = 2.5 \times 30 \times 60 = 4500 \text{ C}$$

Turn charge into moles of $\text{CO}_{2}$**
One mole of electrons carries $96500 \text{ C}$. The equation shows $6\text{e}^{-}$ give $1\text{CO}_{2}$: $$\text{CH}_{3}\text{OH} + \text{H}_{2}\text{O} \rightarrow \text{CO}_{2} + 6\text{H}^{+} + 6\text{e}^{-}$$ So $$n(\text{CO}_{2}) = \frac{Q}{6F} = \frac{4500}{6 \times 96500} = 7.77 \times 10^{-3} \text{ mol}$$

Convert moles of gas to volume**
At room conditions one mole of gas occupies $24000 \text{ cm}^{3}$: $$V = n \times 24000 = 7.77 \times 10^{-3} \times 24000 = 187 \text{ cm}^{3}$$ This is the volume of $\text{CO}_{2}$ released at the anode.

Final answer: $Q = 2.5 \times 30 \times 60 = 4500 \text{ C}$
Moles $\text{e}^{-} = 4500/96500$, moles $\text{CO}_{2} = 4500/(6 \times 96500) = 7.77 \times 10^{-3} \text{ mol}$
Volume $\text{CO}_{2} = 7.77 \times 10^{-3} \times 24000 = 187 \text{ cm}^{3}$
